paragraphs.heading: Climate before thermometers
paragraphs.text: Paleoclimatology is the science of climates from before people invented weather instruments, when nobody was taking direct measurements. Instrument records cover only a sliver of Earth's history, so rebuilding ancient climates helps us see how climate varies naturally and how today's climate came to be. To do it, researchers use proxies: clues kept in rocks, sediments, boreholes, ice sheets, tree rings, corals, shells and microfossils. Once those clues are dated, the records reveal what Earth's atmosphere was like in the past.

paragraphs.heading: Why the past matters now
paragraphs.text: Researchers study periods such as Earth's many glaciations, sudden cold spells like the Younger Dryas, and the fast warming of the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum. Work on past changes in environments and living things often speaks to the present, especially how climate shaped mass extinctions and the recovery of life afterward, and how that relates to global warming today. Late in the 20th century, scientists added a new aim: finding ancient climates that resemble ours and can tell us something about current climate change.

paragraphs.heading: The short instrument record
paragraphs.text: Direct measurement is the most straightforward way to see a climate change, and comparing newer data with older data gives a basic picture of how weather and climate in an area have shifted. The catch is time. Climate data were first recorded in the mid-1800s, which leaves researchers only about 150 years to work with. That does little to map what an area was like 10,000 years ago, and that gap is where more complex methods come in.

paragraphs.heading: Air sealed in ice
paragraphs.text: Mountain glaciers and the polar ice sheets hold a large share of the data. Ice cores drilled in Greenland and Antarctica reach back several hundred thousand years, and the EPICA project went past 800,000 years. As each year's snow piles on and presses older snow into ice, air gets locked in tiny bubbles, which can be measured to learn directly what the air contained when that ice formed. Seasonal pauses in snowfall leave visible layers, so a given depth in the core can be matched to a span of time, and changes in layer thickness point to changes in temperature or precipitation.

paragraphs.heading: Clues in oxygen and pollen
paragraphs.text: Ice layers also carry a chemical signal. Water containing the heavier oxygen-18 evaporates at a higher temperature than water with ordinary oxygen-16, so shifts in the amount of oxygen-18 (δ¹⁸O) in the ice track changes in average ocean surface temperature. The ratio climbs as temperature rises, though it also depends on things like how salty the water is and how much water is tied up in ice sheets. Pollen trapped in the ice shows which plants were growing when a layer formed, and counting grains by shape in a measured sample gives a pollen count for that layer.

paragraphs.heading: Older records fade
paragraphs.text: The method chosen depends on what is being rebuilt, such as temperature or rainfall, and how far back the climate of interest lies. The deep sea floor supplies most isotope data, but it sits on ocean plates that are eventually pulled under, so the oldest material left is 200 million years old. Older sediments also suffer more change from diagenesis, after millions of years of pressure, tectonic activity and fluid flowing through the rock. As a result, the data tend to be thinner or poorer the further back one looks, and confidence drops with age.
